message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the most important rights and protections that Texas tenants enjoy under state law. This is not legal advice, but a general guide. For specific situations—especially if you’re dealing with a landlord dispute, eviction, or a lease that contains unusual clauses—consult a qualified attorney or the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | Area | Key Rights & Protections | How to Exercise Them | |------|--------------------------|----------------------| | **Security Deposits** | • Landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a residential unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after the tenant vacates, unless the landlord provides a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request the deposit return in writing. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a **reasonable time** after notice. | • Document problems (photos, written notice).
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent (in limited circumstances) or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords may raise rent **once per year** and must give **30 days’ written notice**.
• No “no‑increase” clause can be enforced if the lease is for a term of less than a year. | • Review your lease for any “no‑increase” clause; if it’s a month‑to‑month lease, the landlord can still raise rent with proper notice. | | **Eviction** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** (30 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violation, 60 days for no‑cause eviction in month‑to‑month).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• File a **“Notice to Pay Rent or Quit”** or “Notice to Cure or Quit” if you’re behind on rent or violating the lease. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord may enter the premises **only** for:
1. Repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers.
2. In emergencies.
3. With **24‑hour written notice** for non‑emergency reasons. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or other protected classes. | • Report discrimination to the Texas Attorney General’s Office or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing for any term longer than one year.
• The lease cannot contain **unreasonable or illegal** provisions (e.g., “no pets” if the unit is a multi‑family dwelling). | • Read the lease carefully before signing. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may **deduct the cost** from your rent (up to the amount of the repair) and pay the landlord in installments. | • Keep receipts and provide written notice to the landlord. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. | • Rent increases are governed by the lease and the 30‑day notice rule. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide **heat, hot water, and electricity** unless otherwise specified. | • Verify which utilities are included in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Tenants may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s **written consent** (unless the lease allows it). | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Move‑Out Inspection** | • Landlord may conduct a move‑out inspection, but must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours). | • Conduct a walk‑through with the landlord and document any damages. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If a landlord violates your rights, you can file a **small‑claims case** (up to $20,000) or a civil suit in district court. | • Keep all documentation (lease, receipts, correspondence). | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read the Lease** – Understand rent amount, due date, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know Your Notice Requirements** – 30‑day notice for rent increase, 30‑day notice for nonpayment, 60‑day notice for no‑cause eviction in month‑to‑month. 4. **Respond Promptly** – If you receive a notice, reply in writing and keep copies. 5. **Seek Help Early** – Contact the Texas Attorney General’s Office, local tenant‑rights groups, or a lawyer if you face eviction or discrimination. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Housing** | Tenant‑landlord information, complaint filing, and legal guidance. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on fair housing, landlord‑tenant laws, and housing assistance. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal clinics, mediation services, and advocacy. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Process for filing claims up to $20,000. | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | Fair housing enforcement and resources. | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, reasonable notice before rent increases or eviction, protection against discrimination, and the ability to withhold rent or pursue legal remedies if your landlord fails to meet obligations. Always keep records, communicate in writing, and seek professional help if you encounter disputes.
